exec_comm.label: Executive communication
exec_comm.description: Bottom line first for senior leaders; business impact over technical detail.
exec_comm.great: Headline in the first sentence, one or two facts in business terms, then a clear decision or ask.

tech_translation.label: Technical translation
tech_translation.description: Explaining complex technology to non-technical or skeptical audiences.
tech_translation.great: One vivid analogy, why it matters to this listener, zero unexplained jargon, an honest limit.

discovery.label: Customer discovery
discovery.description: Finding the real problem behind the request, scoping, defining success.
discovery.great: Curious, names the questions you would ask, reframes the symptom into the root problem, defines measurable success.

pushback.label: Saying no & scope control
pushback.description: Declining or reshaping requests while protecting the relationship.
pushback.great: Acknowledge the need, name the trade-off plainly, offer a real alternative, keep the door open.

crisis.label: Incidents & bad news
crisis.description: Outages, failures, slips and bad news delivered under pressure.
crisis.great: Own it early; facts, impact, what is being done, when they hear next. Calm pace, no blame.

influence.label: Influence without authority
influence.description: Moving product, engineering, research, sales and security teams you do not manage.
influence.great: Customer evidence, a framing that serves their goals too, and one specific ask.

prioritization.label: Prioritization & trade-offs
prioritization.description: Choosing under constraint and explaining what you will not do.
prioritization.great: Explicit criteria, a decisive choice, what gets dropped and how you will tell people.

ownership.label: Ownership & failure
ownership.description: Behavioral stories and moments of accountability.
ownership.great: Specific story (situation, action, result, lesson), owns their part without self-flagellation, shows the change made.

trust_ethics.label: Trust, security & ethics
trust_ethics.description: Data, safety, honesty and policy lines with customers and colleagues.
trust_ethics.great: A clear principled line, transparent reasoning, protects the customer and the company, offers a safe path forward.

leadership.label: Leadership & vision
leadership.description: Leading teams, mentoring, morale and a point of view on the FDE craft.
leadership.great: A clear stance, a concrete example, and words that would make a team want to follow.

commercial.label: Commercial & negotiation
commercial.description: Value, renewals, pricing pressure and expansion conversations.
commercial.great: Anchor on measured value, trade rather than concede, end with a concrete next step.

ambiguity.label: Ambiguity & judgment calls
ambiguity.description: Unclear requirements, broken environments and decisions with incomplete information.
ambiguity.great: States assumptions, makes a call, says how they will validate it and when they will revisit.

frameworks.explain: Headline → Analogy → Why it matters to them

constraints.text: Lead with your recommendation in the first sentence.
No jargon: your listener is non-technical.
Use exactly three points, and say “three” up front.
Include one specific number or metric.
End with a clear ask or next step.
Acknowledge their perspective before you give yours.
Finish in 45 seconds, then stop and hold the silence.
Do not apologize more than once.
Name one risk and how you will manage it.
Speak as if the CEO just joined the call.
Name the lesson in one sentence at the end.
Tell it in under 30 seconds of setup, then spend the rest on what you did.
State the one assumption you are making, then commit.

questions.text: In one minute, tell a VP of Operations what a Forward Deployed Engineer does and why she should want one on her project.
Summarize the last project you worked on for a CEO who has 60 seconds between meetings.
The customer’s COO asks you in the elevator: “Is this AI project actually going to save us money, or is it a science experiment?” Answer her.
Give a status update to your executive sponsor: the project is on track, but one integration is at risk.
You are presenting results to the customer’s leadership. The CFO interrupts on slide two: “Skip to the part where you tell me the ROI.” You don’t have a hard ROI number yet. Respond.
Your executive sponsor asks you to present to their board next week and to “make it sound further along than it is.” Respond to the sponsor.
Your pilot succeeded with one team. Make the case to the CIO for rolling it out to five more teams next quarter.
Halfway through the quarterly review, the customer’s CEO says: “Honestly, my people don’t use this. Why should I renew?” Respond in the room.
You have one minute with a new CTO who inherited your project and is skeptical of every vendor her predecessor chose. Win her attention.
At an all-hands with 200 of the customer’s employees, someone asks: “Is this AI going to replace our jobs?” The executive who invited you turns to you. Answer.
The customer’s CEO calls you directly, bypassing your leadership, and asks for your honest opinion on whether your company’s roadmap will meet their needs. You have real doubts. Respond.
Explain what an API is to a hospital administrator who has never written code.
Explain the difference between a pilot and a production deployment to a business stakeholder.
Explain why the AI model sometimes gives confident but wrong answers to a customer service manager whose team will use it every day.
A procurement lead asks why the integration will take six weeks when “it’s just connecting two systems.” Explain.
Explain to a skeptical legal team how their data flows through the system: what is stored, where, and for how long, without drowning them in detail.
The head of sales asks why the model can’t “just learn from our CRM overnight.” Explain retrieval, fine-tuning and prompting in plain language.
An operations director says: “Your system is 94% accurate. That means it’s wrong 6% of the time. Why would I trust it?” Respond.
Explain latency versus cost trade-offs to a CFO who wants the fastest and the cheapest option at the same time.
A board member with no technical background asks you to explain, in one minute, how you know the AI system is safe to use with customer data. Answer him.
Mid-demo, the customer’s most senior engineer says loudly: “This is just a wrapper around someone else’s model. What’s actually hard here?” The room goes quiet. Answer him.
Explain to a room of tired, skeptical nurses why they should trust an AI tool that summarizes patient notes, and what they should never trust it to do.
What are the first three questions you ask when you meet a new customer, and why those three?
How do you figure out what a customer actually needs when what they ask for is a specific feature?
A customer says: “We want a chatbot.” Walk them toward the real problem they are trying to solve, out loud, in your own words.
The executive sponsor gives you a vague goal: “Make our analysts more productive with AI.” Turn it into something measurable, speaking to the sponsor.
The customer’s team lead insists the problem is the model. Your early data says the real problem is messy source data owned by another department. Tell her.
The customer has defined success as “users like it.” Explain why that is risky and propose better success criteria.
Two customer departments want your time and each claims their use case is the priority. In a joint meeting, facilitate how you will decide.
Three weeks into discovery, you realize the use case the customer bought the product for won’t deliver meaningful value. Tell the executive sponsor.
Frontline users tell you privately that the workflow leadership described doesn’t match how work actually gets done. Raise it with leadership without throwing the users under the bus.
The customer’s VP says: “We don’t have time for discovery. Just build what we asked for.” You believe that will fail. Respond.
At kickoff, the customer’s CIO and CISO openly disagree about whether the project should exist at all. They ask for your view. Respond.
How do you say no to a customer without damaging the relationship? Give your approach.
Tell me about a time you pushed back on a request. What happened?
A customer asks for “just one more small feature” two days before go-live. Respond.
A customer engineer asks you to give his team admin access to your company’s internal tools “to move faster.” Decline and offer a path.
Your executive sponsor asks you to commit to a launch date that your engineers say is impossible. Respond in the meeting.
Your own sales team promised a customer a capability the product doesn’t have. The customer brings it up with you. Respond to the customer.
The customer wants the product customized so heavily it would become a one-off fork nobody can maintain. Say no and redirect them.
A customer threatens to escalate to your CEO unless you commit your team to weekend work for a non-critical feature. Respond.
Your manager asks you to take on a third customer deployment. You’re already at capacity and quality is slipping. Respond to your manager.
In front of her team, the customer’s CEO says: “Your competitor said they could do this in half the time. Why can’t you?” You know their promise is unrealistic. Respond without trashing them.
A major customer asks you to disable a safety filter because it is “blocking legitimate work.” Some of their examples are valid; some are not. Respond.
What is your first move when something breaks in production at a customer site?
Tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news. How did you do it?
A bug in your deployment sent incorrect summaries to 30 users this morning. Say, out loud, your first message to the customer’s project lead.
The demo you’re giving to the customer’s leadership crashes in the first minute. Say what you say next.
An outage has blocked the customer’s support team for three hours during their busiest week. Their director calls you, angry. Respond.
You discover a data pipeline you built has silently dropped 10% of records for two weeks. Nobody has noticed yet. Tell the customer.
The go-live you have promised for a month is going to slip two weeks. Tell the executive sponsor.
The AI system gave one of the customer’s end users harmful advice, and a screenshot is circulating inside the customer. Their head of communications is on the phone. Respond.
You’re on-site. The customer’s VP pulls you aside: “If this outage happens again, we’re done.” Your team doesn’t know the root cause yet. Respond.
A critical incident was caused by a configuration change you made. In the post-mortem with the customer’s executives, the CTO asks: “Whose fault is this?” Answer.
On a live incident call with 20 people, including the customer’s CIO, your own engineering lead contradicts what you just told the customer. Respond on the call.
How do you get engineers who don’t report to you to prioritize your customer’s problem?
Explain why feedback from the field should shape a product roadmap.
Pitch your product team, in one minute, on building a feature three of your customers keep asking for.
A research team built a model improvement, but they don’t see why your customer’s edge case matters. Convince them.
Your product manager says your customer’s request is “too niche.” You believe it signals a pattern across the market. Make the case.
You need the security team to fast-track a review that normally takes six weeks, or the deal stalls. Ask them.
Two senior engineers disagree about the architecture for a customer deployment and it is blocking progress. Get them aligned.
Leadership is about to deprioritize a product area your biggest customer depends on. You get one minute in the meeting. Make your case.
Sales wants you to commit engineering time to a prospect you believe is a poor fit. The sales VP outranks you. Respond to him.
In a leadership meeting, a senior executive dismisses field feedback as “anecdotes.” You have strong evidence. Respond without making it personal.
Your research team wants to feature your customer’s deployment as a public case study. The customer hasn’t agreed and is sensitive about it. Speak to the research lead.
How do you decide what to work on first when everything seems urgent?
Walk through how you plan your first week at a new customer site.
You have two days before a demo and three unfinished features. Tell your customer contact which one you’re cutting and why.
Is it better to ship a rough solution this week or a polished one next month? Take a side, using a real customer scenario.
Two customers escalate on the same afternoon: one has a production bug, the other has an executive demo tomorrow. You can handle one personally. Decide and explain it to the other.
A customer wants 12 use cases in the first quarter. Explain how you would pick the first two.
Your manager asks why you spent a week on internal tooling instead of customer features. Defend it or concede it; decide.
Your biggest customer wants a feature that would pull your only other engineer off a smaller customer’s launch. Make the call and tell both parties.
You are asked to cut your deployment budget by 40% and keep the same outcomes. What do you cut, and how do you explain it?
Friday, 5 p.m.: a security patch, a customer go-live and a promised executive report all need you this weekend. Tell your manager what you will and won’t do.
The customer’s executive says: “Everything on this list is priority one.” Push her to force-rank it, in the meeting.
Tell me about a mistake you made at work and what you changed afterward.
Tell me about a time you went beyond your role to help a customer or teammate succeed.
Tell me about a project that failed. What was your part in it?
Describe a time you received tough feedback. What did you do with it?
Tell me about a decision you made with incomplete information that turned out wrong. How did you recover?
You shipped a feature customers aren’t using. Your manager asks what happened. Answer honestly.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager and you were the one who was wrong.
You missed a commitment to a customer because you overcommitted across projects. Apologize to the customer and reset expectations.
Tell me about the hardest professional conversation you’ve had. What would you do differently?
A junior engineer’s error hurt a customer, but you approved the change. With the junior engineer in the room, the customer’s executive asks who is accountable. Answer.
In your review, your manager says customers love you but internal teams find you difficult to work with. Respond.
What does it mean to be a trusted advisor to a customer rather than just a vendor?
When is it acceptable to tell a customer “I don’t know”?
A customer asks you to copy their production customer data into a quick test environment “just for today.” Respond.
The customer asks whether your AI system is “unbiased.” Give an honest answer.
A customer wants to use your AI system to screen job applicants automatically with no human review. Respond.
You learn the customer tells its end users that no AI is involved in a process that uses your system. Raise it with your contact.
A customer engineer pastes production credentials into a chat with you “to save time.” Respond, and fix it.
Your sales lead asks you to downplay a known product limitation in a customer’s security questionnaire. Respond to the sales lead.
A customer wants to use the system where a wrong answer could harm someone’s health, and is pushing to launch next week. Respond.
A customer executive offers a much bigger contract if you help them use the system in a way that likely violates your company’s usage policy. Respond.
A journalist contacts you directly about a rumored failure at one of your customers. You know some of the details. Respond to the journalist.
What makes a great Forward Deployed Engineer different from a great software engineer?
Describe the best leader you’ve worked with and what you learned from them.
How would you onboard a new engineer onto a messy, high-pressure customer deployment?
What does good leadership look like when you have no formal authority?
Your team just lost a major customer after months of work. Morale is low. Say what you would say to the team on Monday morning.
Take a position: should Forward Deployed Engineers specialize by industry or stay generalists? Defend it.
A high-performing teammate is burning out but insists they’re fine. Talk to them.
If you were building an FDE team from scratch next year, what would you do differently from how most teams operate today?
Your team is split: half want to build a reusable platform, half want to keep shipping custom solutions. Set the direction.
In five years the FDE role will be either the most important role in the company or gone. Pick one and defend it.
You were just promoted to lead the team. A former peer who wanted the role openly questions your decision in a meeting. Respond in the meeting.
How do you show a customer the value of a deployment in their language, not yours?
What is an engineer’s role in closing or expanding a deal?
A customer asks for a discount because the pilot “took longer than expected.” Respond.
Your pilot saved one team 10 hours a week. Turn that into an expansion pitch for the customer’s operations leader.
The customer’s procurement lead says: “We like the product, but your competitor is 30% cheaper.” Respond.
The customer asks for six months of free professional services as a condition of renewal. Respond.
Your champion at the customer is leaving the company next month. Talk to her about how to protect the project.
Renewal is in three weeks, usage is down 40%, and your executive sponsor has gone quiet. You get her on the phone. What do you say?
A customer wants payment to depend on a metric you can’t fully control. Respond.
The customer’s CFO says: “Give me one number that proves this was worth it, or we cancel.” Respond.
In a negotiation, the customer’s executive says: “You need our logo more than we need your product.” Respond.
How do you make progress when requirements are unclear?
What do you do in your first hour on-site at a customer you know nothing about?
You arrive on-site and the access, data and hardware you were promised aren’t ready. Tell your manager your plan for the week.
The customer can’t agree on what success means. What do you do tomorrow morning?
The customer’s project lead and your own account executive give you conflicting instructions. Decide what you’ll do and tell both.
You have 48 hours to decide whether to build a custom solution or wait for an official product feature. Make the call and justify it.
The customer’s data is far worse than expected and nobody owns cleaning it. Propose a path in the steering meeting.
Starting tomorrow you own a failing deployment at a customer you have never worked with. You get one call with the account team today. What do you say on that call?
Your product changes monthly, and the customer wants a 12-month roadmap commitment. Respond with a plan.
The executive who championed your project was just fired, and nobody knows if the project continues. You meet her replacement tomorrow. Open that meeting.
Two hours before an executive demo, you find the numbers on your key slide come from a flawed analysis. Decide what to do and say it to your account executive.
